Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
404 AM EST Thu Nov 26 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
The forecast for this powerful Thanksgiving Day system is
largely on track. The biggest change is an uptick in forecast
rainfall amounts. Earlier totals were around 1 to 3 inches which
have now pushed into the 2 to 4 inch range. Consequently, the
Weather Prediction Center expanded the Slight Risk for excessive
rainfall to the Blue Ridge Mountains. Otherwise, Winter Weather
Advisories continue until 9 AM this morning due to light
freezing rain accretions over western portions of the
Alleghenies.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) A powerful coastal low is set to bring hazardous wind,
  tidal flooding, and heavy rain on Thanksgiving Day.

- 2) Drier conditions this weekend, followed by additional
  precipitation chances early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...A powerful coastal low is set to bring hazardous
wind, tidal flooding, and heavy rain on Thanksgiving Day.

A high-impact system is already beginning to move across the
region early this morning. Throughout this Thanksgiving Day,
expect strong northeasterly winds, tidal flooding, and heavy
rainfall. A number of hazardous weather products have been
issued for many of these threats (referenced further within Key
Message 1, the Marine section, and the Tides/Coastal Flooding).

Starting aloft, an expansive region of lower heights stretches
from the Ozarks over to the southeastern U.S. Two discrete
cyclonic circulations exist, one swirling over Arkansas while
the other feature spins across the Florida Panhandle. This lead
wave will quickly lift up the Carolina coast while attaining a
negative tilt. As a result, the net result will be a deepening
area of surface low pressure which rides the Carolina to Mid-
Atlantic coast today. Per the 06Z surface analysis, this
particular wave has a pressure of 1001 mb and is positioned
about 75 to 100 miles off the coast of Myrtle Beach, South
Carolina. Gradual deepening of this system is expected while the
overall circulation and wind fields expand as the cyclone
occludes. By this evening, the primary low will sit over
southern West Virginia, while the triple point low lifts
northward over the Delmarva Peninsula. By tonight, all of the
action eventually shifts north of the Mason-Dixon Line.

Radar imagery as of 08Z/3 AM shows a band of light to moderate
rain edging north to northwest across the area. Surface
temperatures remain in the upper 30s to 40s which is making for
a cold November rain. The one exception is along western
portions of the Alleghenies where surface temperatures range
from 28 to 32 degrees. With a warm nose just above the surface,
this is yielding some light freezing rain. Consequently, Winter
Weather Advisories run until 9 AM across western sections of
Highland, Grant, and Pendleton counties. If traveling early this
morning, many roads across these areas are seeing light freezing
rain accretions. Until temperatures can rebound to above
freezing, travel issues will remain.

A brunt of the rainfall today is expected to occur in the 7 AM 
to 7 PM window. The latest forecast package indicates around
1.50 to 2.50 inches of rain will impact much of the area. Given
the strong gradient formed by a stout 1040-mb over northern New
England and low pressure near the Carolinas, much of this rain
will be wind driven. Although drought conditions should quell
a more widespread hydrologic response, spotty flooding issues
cannot be ruled out. This would particularly be the case around
urbanized areas, low-lying spots, and anywhere storm drains are
clogged with leaves. Highly anomalous precipitable waters on the
order of 1.50 to 1.75 inches will support hefty rainfall rates
at times. Peak hourly rates could push into the 0.50 to 0.75
inch range. While instability is almost non-existent, the
intense dynamics with this trough could produce spotty low
topped thunderstorms. The Storm Prediction Center does place far
southern Maryland in a Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms.
This would be a brief spin up tornado given the extreme shear in
place. While a brunt of the more widespread rainfall ends during
this evening, the trailing upper low will bring additional
activity to the Potomac Highlands by tonight. 

One thing that makes this system highly anomalous is the intense
vertical wind field. This is already evident on the VAD-wind
profilers from radars to the south. The KAKQ radar in
southeastern Virginia shows 40 to 45 knots of northeasterly 
wind around 1,000 feet, while the 2,000 to 4,000 foot layer
consists of easterlies around 60 to 70 knots. Based on radars
across the Carolinas, a further uptick in these winds is
expected. On the broader scale, the combination of a 1040-mb
high over northern New England and 1001-mb low off the Carolinas
is already fostering decent wind fields. However, the dynamical
forcing within the approaching shortwave will further augment
these background wind fields. By early this afternoon, 925-mb
winds over the region are around 70 to 80 knots, with nearly 100
knots just above at the 850-mb level. One important note is it
will be difficult to fully mix these hurricane force winds down
to the surface despite all the water-laden downdrafts. Forecast
soundings show a rather stable saturated profile which limits
the potential of mixing the more intense winds down to the
ground. The one exception would be the Alleghenies and Blue
Ridge which sit close to that 925-mb level. High Wind Warnings
are in effect given gusts up to 65 mph, with 70 to 75 mph winds
possible at 3,500 feet and above. Elsewhere, High Wind Warnings
also span counties adjacent to the Chesapeake Bay where gusts up
to 60 mph are possible. For all others, Wind Advisories are in
place with northeasterly gusts up to around 55 mph. Overall,
these area-wide strong winds will blow around unsecured 
objects. Additionally, downed trees and power outages are also 
possible.

Heading into Friday, the focus shifts to the Allegheny Front as
an extended period of upslope aided rain/snow showers will 
occur. Deep-layered westerlies are not the most ideal with 
upslope, but net snow accumulations around an inch or two are in
the forecast. Otherwise, the big story for the day will be 
another round of brisk winds across the entire area. Initial 
winds start off out of the south on Friday morning before 
shifting over to west to southwesterly for the second half of 
the day. The passage of the upper low should make for an 
expansive stratocumulus deck which offset some of the daytime 
heating. After spending Thanksgiving Day in the 40s and 50s, 
expect much of the same for Friday (30s along the Alleghenies). 
Southwesterly winds will gust around 25 to 35 mph, while 
remaining elevated into Friday night over the higher terrain. 
Westerly gusts overnight could approach 40 to 50 mph along the 
Allegheny Front. 

The powerful Thanksgiving Day system finally reaches the
Canadian Maritimes by Saturday. This will provide increasing
sunshine through the day, much less wind, along with a gradual 
warm up. Saturday's forecast highs are in the 50s to near 60 
degrees, with upper 30s to 40s across mountain locations. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions this weekend, followed by additional 
precipitation chances early next week.

A brief period of weak mid-level ridging will build overhead this 
weekend in the immediate afermath of the coastal low, which should 
bring sunnier skies with diminishing winds overall. Temperatures 
generally trend upward during this period, with 850mb temp anomalies 
trending 4-8 degrees C above climatological normals Sunday with 
highs in the 50s to low 60s as the surface high begins to slide 
east. 

Meanwhile, upper-level troughing develops over the Midwest and 
begins tracking towards the Mid-Atlantic late Sunday night & into 
Monday. As the associated cold front tracks through, scattered 
showers become possible again along with a brief increase in the 
winds. Depending on the timing & duration of the front, some 
mountain snow could be possible as the trough tracks offshore late 
Monday night and overnight temperatures cool considerably into the 
upper 20s to low 30s. 

Upper-level zonal flow prevails after the passage of the cold front 
next week, with surface high pressure building overhead. Some early 
guidance points to another weak trough moving through the 
area sometime midweek, but will continue to monitor how this 
continues to trend in the meantime

&&

.AVIATION /07Z THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Lengthy restrictions are likely across all terminals as a highly
anomalous system impacts the Eastern Seaboard. This will come
with prolonged IFR ceilings and visibilities, very strong
northeasterly low-level wind shear (50 to 65 knots in the lowest
2,000 feet), and surface wind gusts around 40 to 50 knots. As
noted in the TAFs, the strongest of these winds should occur
during the morning and afternoon hours. A brunt of the moderate
to occasionally heavy rain is to occur in the 7 AM to 7 PM
window (likely ending earlier at places as far south as KCHO).
Heading into this evening, some rain will linger but with low
ceilings persisting through the night. After midnight, the
aviation guidance shows some subtle improvements to MVFR are
possible. However, given all of the ground water from rainfall,
some patchy mist or fog may develop overnight.

Moving into Friday, a stratocumulus deck likely will sprawl
across the region as an upper low moves through. The deck should
be high enough to stay out of MVFR levels, but it could be close
at times. Otherwise, the day will be comprised of shifting winds
which begin out of the south before turning more west to
southwesterly for the second half of the day. Gusts up to 25 to
30 knots are expected, but with a gradual downtick into Friday
night as gradients begin to weaken.

VFR conditions are anticipated Saturday and Sunday, with westerly 
winds gusting up to 15-25 knots Saturday afternoon before 
diminishing overnight. Winds shift southerly Sunday. Beginning 
Sunday night into Monday, a cold front could elevate winds between 
15-25 knots and bring scattered showers to terminals, potentially 
causing periods of sub-VFR conditions at times. Winds shift 
northwesterly by Tuesday in the wake of the front.

&&

.MARINE...
A powerful coastal low will make for an extended period of very
dangerous conditions over the waterways. Storm Warnings
currently cover much of these waters given expected gusts up to
50 to 55 knots. Meanwhile, Gale Warnings fill out the middle to
upper tidal Potomac given forecast northeasterly gusts around 40
to 45 knots. In addition to the strong wind fields, wave heights
will be rising into the 4 to 7 foot range (highest over the more
southern waters). While Storm Warnings drop off this evening,
Gale Warnings continue across a majority of the waters through
tonight and into early Friday afternoon. Looking more closely at
the rest of the Friday's forecast, many spots approach gale
force again, particularly across the Chesapeake Bay. Will allow
the next shift to evaluate the situation to see if Gale 
Warnings need to be extended into early Friday evening.
Thereafter, winds drop to advisory levels.
 
Winds stay above SCA thresholds Saturday before diminishing 
overnight into Sunday. Winds shift southerly by Monday, with 
gusts potentially pushing back into SCA thresholds again Monday 
as a cold front brings scattered showers through the region. 
Winds diminish again Tuesday, shifting northerly in the wake of 
the front.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Intense low pressure will move up the Carolina to Mid-Atlantic coast,
with very strong (near record) high pressure to the north. This
results in a period of strong onshore flow. Tide levels will 
rapidly rise today, with a couple headline additions possible 
depending on how quickly the water rises. The current forecast 
calls for peak anomalies of 3 to 4 feet above normal in the 
middle Chesapeake and Potomac, which combined with high 
astronomical tides from the recent full moon, will result in 
moderate tidal flooding. Coastal Flood Warnings have been issued
for these impacted areas. Coastal Flood Advisories have been 
issued for the rest of the Potomac shoreline where significant 
flooding is less common due to the nature of the shoreline. 
Advisories have also been issued for the remaining northern bay 
shoreline as well. The storm should move quickly enough to 
preclude major flooding anywhere.

The heaviest rain may coincide with high tide around southern
Maryland, furthering the flooding risk due to drainage issues
along the coast with fresh plus tidal input today. Further up
the coast, a Coastal Flood Watch remains over Harford County. A
decision will be made shortly in whether to upgrade to warnings
and move to advisories.

Winds shift around to the west and southwest tonight into 
Friday, which isn't the most favorable for water to quickly 
evacuate the bay. Given the high astronomical tides, this could 
keep a risk of minor to even moderate tidal flooding in the 
picture through Friday night. The excess anomaly will likely 
build toward the northern reaches of the bay at this time. 

Tide levels then drop rapidly Saturday.

&&

.CLIMATE...
Widespread rainfall amounts of 1.5-3 inches are likely to 
result in some new Thanksgiving Day rainfall records. Below is 
the list of the wettest Thanksgiving Days on record. 

Wettest Thanksgiving On Record
Washington-National (DCA)1.15" (11-25-1971) 
Washington-Dulles (IAD)         0.84" (11-24-1983)
Baltimore (BWI)                 1.11" (11-25-1971) 
Baltimore Inner Harbor (DMH)    2.19" (11-25-1971)
Martinsburg (MRB)               0.93" (11-28-1985) 
Charlottesville (CHO)           0.96" (11-28-1935) 
Annapolis(NAK)                  2.72" (11-25-1971) 
Hagerstown (HGR)                1.12" (11-25-1971)

In the approximate 150 years of records for the DC Metro area,
there have only been two Thanksgiving Days with significant
precipitation. Those were in 1971 and 1989 which currently hold
the records for wettest and snowiest Thanksgiving Days on 
record, respectively (one caveat is that Baltimore saw its 
snowiest Thanksgiving back in 1898).

For additional context, only about 1 in 3 Thanksgiving Days on 
record have had measurable precipitation. This holds true across
all of our eight climate stations.
